title: River bike loop
topic: A friend assumes a steady headwind out and tailwind back cancel out on an out-and-back ride
blurb: A friend is timing an out-and-back ride before dinner.
prompt: A friend just sent this in the group chat. Tap a line if something doesn't add up, or let it pass.

segments.label: The route
segments.text: Doing a quick 24-mile ride along the river path before dinner — 12 miles out to the dam and 12 miles straight back.

segments.label: The wind
segments.text: Steady wind down the valley today, so I'm figuring 8 mph pushing out and 16 mph flying back.

segments.label: The math
segments.text: Works out to my usual 12 mph average, so rolling out at 4:00 gets me back in the shower by 6:00.

segments.label: The take
segments.text: Still plenty of time to make our 6:30 table.

conclusion: 8 mph out and 16 mph back averages 12 mph, so rolling out at 4:00 gets me home by 6:00.

flaws.original: 12 miles at 8 mph takes 1.5 hours and 12 miles back at 16 mph takes 45 minutes — that's 2 hours 15 minutes, so you won't get home until 6:15.
flaws.corrupted: Works out to my usual 12 mph average, so rolling out at 4:00 gets me back in the shower by 6:00.

diagnosis_choices.label: 12 miles at 8 mph is 1.5h and back at 16 mph is 45m — you get home at 6:15, not 6:00.
Air drag grows with speed squared, so a headwind slows you more than 4 mph and puts you back at 6:20.
12 miles at 8 mph is 1.5h and 12 miles at 16 mph is 0.5h, which hits 6:00 only with zero turnaround stop.
Your average speed is 12 mph only if you ride the tailwind leg first and save your legs for the climb back.

fix_choices.label: Add the two leg times (1.5h + 0.75h = 2h 15m): roll out at 3:45 to be back by 6:00.
Use 7 mph out and 15 mph back to model air drag, and leave 20 minutes earlier.
Start with the tailwind first so you bank speed before turning around at the dam.
Turn around at 5:00 sharp instead of the 12-mile dam so both halves take one hour.

flaws.explanation: You spend 1.5 hours grinding at 8 mph and only 45 minutes flying back at 16 mph — 2 hours 15 minutes total, so you won't walk in until 6:15.
flaws.why_tempting: 8 and 16 average straight to 12, and 24 ÷ 12 = 2 hours feels seamless. You only catch it when you time each 12-mile leg separately.
flaws.catch_rule: When two legs cover the same distance at different speeds, compute the time for each leg separately — the slower leg always drags the total down.
flaws.hint: How long does 12 miles at 8 mph take? Now how long does 12 miles back at 16 mph take?

practice.problem: A ferry crosses a 6-mile channel at 6 mph against the current and returns 6 miles at 12 mph with it. Does the round trip average 9 mph?
practice.answer: No — 1 hour out plus 0.5 hours back is 1.5 hours for 12 miles, which is 8 mph, not 9.

diagnosis: 12 miles out and 12 miles back at 12 mph is 2 hours only if you turn around instantaneously with zero pause.
A 24-mile round trip at 12 mph takes 2.4 hours, not 2 hours, once you include the turnaround.
Cruising at 12 mph normally means your average speed is slower than 12 mph because of starts and stops.
You can't compare a windy ride against a calm 2-hour baseline without knowing the trail's elevation gain.
fix: Add a 10-minute water break at the 12-mile mark before timing the ride.
Measure the trail's slope before assuming both legs take the same effort.
Use your door-to-door pace instead of cruising speed as the baseline.
Check whether the river trail is 12 miles total or 12 miles each way.

diagnosis: A 4 mph wind doesn't simply subtract 4 and add 4 to your bike speed — rolling resistance stays fixed.
If the wind blows down the river, going 8 mph out and 16 mph back means the wind was 8 mph, not 4.
Headwinds usually shift direction over two hours, so assuming a steady 4 mph wind invalidates the whole ride.
12 minus 4 is 8 and 12 plus 4 is 16, which is a 2× speed gap — too wide for a mild 4 mph breeze.
fix: Estimate 10 mph out and 14 mph back instead of adding and subtracting the full 4 mph.
Check the forecast to see if the wind drops before your return leg.
Note that an 8-to-16 mph swing actually corresponds to an 8 mph wind.
Use a power meter instead of adding and subtracting wind speed directly.

diagnosis: Wind doesn't slow you down on a flat out-and-back, it just makes the outbound half feel harder.
Wind actually speeds you up overall on an out-and-back because 16 mph is double 8 mph.
Wind only slows you down if it blows across the trail as a crosswind, not straight along it.
Calling a 2-hour ride unaffected ignores that your legs are twice as tired after 8 mph.
fix: Say wind costs extra effort even though the clock stays at 2 hours.
Check whether the wind is a crosswind before assuming it cancels out.
Acknowledge that fighting 8 mph drains your legs before the tailwind starts.
Flip the claim: a headwind-tailwind out-and-back always takes longer than a calm day.

clean_segments: Doing a quick 24-mile ride along the river path before dinner — 12 miles out to the dam and 12 miles straight back.
Steady wind down the valley today, so I'm figuring 8 mph pushing out and 16 mph flying back.
12 miles at 8 mph takes 1.5 hours and 12 miles back at 16 mph takes 45 minutes — that's 2 hours 15 minutes, so you won't get home until 6:15.
Still plenty of time to make our 6:30 table.
clean_conclusion: 1.5 hours out plus 45 minutes back puts you home at 6:15, not 6:00.
